nameStory: Small Pussytoes gets its charming name from its fuzzy flower heads that look remarkably like tiny cat paws or kitten toes. The soft, woolly white texture of both the flowers and leaf undersides gives the whole plant a distinctly feline, touchable appearance. It's also called 'everlasting' because the papery flowers hold their shape and color long after drying.
description: Small Pussytoes is a low-growing perennial wildflower that forms neat rosettes of spoon-shaped leaves close to the ground. The plant stays evergreen through winter and sends up slender flower stems in spring, reaching only about a foot tall at most. Its most distinctive features are the cluster of small, fuzzy white flower heads that really do look like miniature cat paws, and the leaves with their silvery-white woolly undersides. This modest little plant spreads by underground runners to form small colonies.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small clusters of fuzzy white flower heads that feel soft and cottony to the touch, appearing in May on stems 6-14 inches tall. Each tiny flower head is about the size of a pencil eraser and has a distinctly cat-paw-like appearance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Spoon-shaped basal leaves 1-2 inches long with broad rounded tips, light green on top but distinctly woolly white underneath. Run your finger along the underside to feel the soft, fuzzy texture that's unmistakable.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low rosettes that hug the ground, staying green through winter. Plants spread by runners to create small patches or colonies rather than growing as isolated individuals.

idTips.label: Stem Leaves
idTips.description: The flowering stems have much smaller, narrower leaves than the basal rosette - these are only about an inch long and feel thin between your fingers.

habitat: Look for Small Pussytoes in sandy or well-drained soils, especially under pine forests where the canopy is fairly open. It thrives in slightly acidic conditions and is often found on slopes, clearings, and woodland edges throughout New England's mountains and hills. This plant particularly loves spots where the soil stays somewhat dry and doesn't get waterlogged.

seasonality.spring: Flowers bloom in May, sending up their characteristic fuzzy white flower heads on slender stems. This is the easiest time to spot and identify the plant.
seasonality.summer: Flowers may persist into early summer, gradually becoming more papery but retaining their shape. The basal leaves remain green and visible.
seasonality.fall: The evergreen rosettes stay fresh and green, making this a good time to observe the distinctive spoon-shaped leaves with their woolly white undersides.
seasonality.winter: Unlike most wildflowers, the basal rosettes remain green and visible under snow, making it one of the few evergreen wildflowers you can find in New England winters.

funFact: Small Pussytoes is a master of cloning - most populations are entirely female plants that reproduce by sending out underground runners, creating genetically identical colonies that can persist for decades without ever producing seeds!
confusionNotes: The other pussytoes species in New England can look very similar, but Small Pussytoes is typically the most compact with the smallest leaves. Field Pussytoes tends to be taller and larger overall, while Plantain-leaved Pussytoes has distinctly ribbed leaves. When in doubt, focus on the overall size - if everything looks miniaturized, you've likely found Small Pussytoes.
contextualKnowledge: The species name 'howellii' honors Thomas J. Howell, an Oregon botanist who first collected this plant in 1887. Interestingly, what we call 'Small Pussytoes' actually has several subspecies across North America, with the northeastern form being subspecies canadensis.
compareHints: Small Pussytoes lives up to its name by being noticeably smaller than its relatives - its leaves are typically under 2 inches long compared to Field Pussytoes which can have 4-inch leaves. The flower clusters are also more compact and closer to the ground. Plantain-leaved Pussytoes has obvious parallel leaf veins that Small Pussytoes lacks, while Parlin's Pussytoes tends to grow in wetter areas.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Field pussytoes differs from small pussytoes by being taller and having more flower heads per cluster.

Among the pussytoes species in New England, plantain-leaved pussytoes is distinguished by its notably broader, more prominently veined leaves compared to field pussytoes or small pussytoes, which have much narrower, less obviously ribbed foliage.
Parlin's pussytoes is generally more robust and taller than Small Pussytoes, and has broader, more spoon-shaped leaves compared to the narrower leaves of Field Pussytoes.
Catsfoot differs from other New England pussytoes by its preference for cooler, mountainous habitats and its particularly silvery-white, woolly appearance.
